title: Modern OAuth/OIDC: IdP, PKCE, STS & OBO
description: A practical map of identity, OAuth 2.1, OpenID Connect, PKCE, security token services, on-behalf-of delegation, hardened profiles, threats, and operations.

root.label: Modern Identity + API Authorization
root.notes: OAuth delegates authorization to protected resources; OIDC adds authentication and identity claims; PKCE binds authorization codes to clients; an STS exchanges credentials across trust boundaries; OBO preserves a user's delegated context through a service chain. Treat tokens as purpose-bound credentials, not interchangeable proof of identity.

children.label: Identity Provider (IdP)
children.notes: The authority that authenticates users and manages identity lifecycle. In OIDC it is the OpenID Provider (OP); it often also operates the OAuth Authorization Server, but those are distinct roles.

children.label: Identity Plane
children.notes: Directories, identity proofing, authenticators, policies, sessions, federation, and lifecycle management establish who a principal is before tokens represent that result.

children.label: Authenticators
children.notes: Prefer phishing-resistant passkeys/WebAuthn or hardware keys for high assurance. Passwords, TOTP, push, and recovery methods should be evaluated as a complete authentication system.

children.label: Identity Lifecycle
children.notes: Joiner/mover/leaver processes, SCIM provisioning, entitlement review, account recovery, and credential reset can be more important than the login protocol itself.

children.label: Assurance Context
children.notes: OIDC acr and amr can describe authentication strength and methods. Treat them as policy inputs only when issuer-specific values and freshness requirements are understood.

children.label: SSO Sessions
children.notes: The IdP's browser cookie provides SSO; the application's own session represents local login state. Neither is an OAuth access token. Logout must consider both layers.

children.label: IdP Cookie
children.notes: Usually scoped to the IdP domain with Secure, HttpOnly, and appropriate SameSite settings. It enables reauthentication without exposing credentials to clients.

children.label: App Session
children.notes: A web app or BFF should normally expose only an opaque, Secure, HttpOnly session cookie to the browser while keeping OAuth tokens server-side.

children.label: Tenants & Issuers
children.notes: Tenant boundaries determine issuer identifiers, policies, directories, and keys. Validate the exact issuer; never infer tenant trust merely from a shared host name.

children.label: Federation & Brokering
children.notes: A broker accepts an upstream identity protocol and issues tokens in a stable local trust domain. Federation changes who authenticates the user, not which audience an API token is valid for.

children.label: SAML Federation
children.notes: Common for workforce browser SSO. A broker can translate a validated SAML assertion into a local OIDC session and tokens without forwarding the assertion to every application.

children.label: OIDC Federation
children.notes: OIDC federation and identity brokering use issuer metadata and cryptographic trust to connect providers. Do not confuse upstream identity federation with downstream API token exchange.

children.label: OAuth 2.1 Authorization
children.notes: OAuth grants a client limited access to a resource. OAuth 2.1 is still an evolving Internet-Draft; it consolidates OAuth 2.0 plus modern security practice rather than introducing a different authorization model.

children.label: Actors & Trust
children.notes: Resource Owner authorizes; Client requests access; Authorization Server (AS) issues tokens; Resource Server (RS) protects APIs. One product may host several roles, but validation must preserve the logical boundaries.

children.label: Public vs Confidential
children.notes: Public clients cannot keep static credentials; SPAs and installed apps are public even if a secret is embedded. Confidential clients authenticate securely at the token endpoint.

children.label: Resource Indicators
children.notes: RFC 8707 resource parameters let a client identify the target protected resource. Issue one narrowly scoped token per resource rather than a universal downstream token.

children.label: Consent vs Policy
children.notes: Consent records a user's authorization choice; it does not replace organizational policy, legal basis, or API authorization checks. First-party and administrator-approved access may use different policy paths.

children.label: Grant Selection
children.notes: Choose a grant from the actor and interaction model. Do not select a flow because a vendor UI happens to expose it.

children.label: Authorization Code
children.notes: The browser carries a short-lived, one-time code; the client redeems it at the token endpoint. Use PKCE, state or an equivalent transaction binding, exact redirects, and OIDC nonce when applicable.

children.label: Client Credentials
children.notes: A workload acts as itself. There is no user and normally no ID token; permissions belong to the client or service principal.

children.label: Device Authorization
children.notes: RFC 8628 supports input-constrained devices and CLIs. The user authorizes on a separate device; polling must respect interval, expiry, and slow_down responses.

children.label: Assertion Grants
children.notes: JWT or SAML bearer assertions can be authorization grants (RFC 7523/7522). Validate issuer, audience, time, signature, and replay identifiers; an assertion grant is distinct from client authentication.

children.label: Do Not Use
children.notes: Implicit exposes tokens through the front channel; Resource Owner Password Credentials trains clients to collect passwords. OAuth Security BCP deprecates both. Use code + PKCE or an appropriate non-password grant.

children.label: Redirect & Transaction Binding
children.notes: Register exact redirect URIs, reject open redirectors, bind callbacks to the initiating browser transaction, and use authorization-server issuer identification where multiple issuers share a client.

children.label: Scopes Are Not Full AuthZ
children.notes: Scopes bound what a client may attempt. The API must still enforce resource ownership, tenant, role, object, relationship, and business rules. Never treat token presence alone as authorization.

children.label: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
children.notes: OIDC is an authentication and identity layer over OAuth. It adds ID tokens, standardized authentication requests and claims, discovery, UserInfo, session/logout specifications, and conformance profiles.

children.label: Authentication Request
children.notes: openid scope activates OIDC. state binds the response to client state; nonce binds the ID token to the request and mitigates replay. prompt, max_age, login_hint, acr_values, and claims refine interaction.

children.label: Step-up Authentication
children.notes: Request stronger or fresher authentication when a sensitive action requires it. Verify returned acr/amr/auth_time against policy; do not assume MFA from a generic claim.

children.label: Reauthentication
children.notes: max_age and prompt=login can request fresh interaction, but the client must validate auth_time and provider behavior. Reauthentication is not the same as re-consent.

children.label: ID Token
children.notes: A signed statement about an authentication event for one client. Validate iss, aud, exp, nonce, signature, and azp when required. Never use an ID token as an API access token.

children.label: Subjects & Claims
children.notes: sub is the stable subject identifier within an issuer; pairwise subjects reduce correlation across clients. email, groups, and names are attributes that can change and are poor database keys.

children.label: Issuer + Subject Key
children.notes: Use the pair (iss, sub) as the external identity key. A sub value is not globally unique and an email address is not a durable identifier.

children.label: Claim Minimization
children.notes: Release only claims the client needs. Large group lists create leakage, stale authorization, and token-size problems; prefer API-side entitlement lookup for complex policy.

children.label: Discovery & Registration
children.notes: The .well-known configuration publishes issuer, endpoints, supported algorithms, and jwks_uri. Pin the expected issuer and apply secure dynamic registration policy; metadata is not blanket trust.

children.label: JWKS & Key Rotation
children.notes: Cache JWKS using HTTP semantics, select keys by kid plus allowed algorithm, refresh on an unknown key with rate limits, and retain overlap during rotation. Never accept keys supplied by an untrusted token header.

children.label: UserInfo
children.notes: A protected endpoint for additional claims. Validate that its sub matches the ID token subject; access-token authorization and privacy policy determine released data.

children.label: OIDC Logout
children.notes: RP-initiated logout begins at a relying party; front-channel and back-channel logout notify clients. Logout UX, application sessions, IdP sessions, and token revocation are separate controls.

children.label: PKCE
children.notes: Proof Key for Code Exchange (RFC 7636) binds an authorization code to the client instance that initiated the request. It mitigates intercepted-code redemption; it is not client authentication and does not replace state, nonce, or redirect validation.

children.label: Threat Addressed
children.notes: If an attacker steals a code from an OS redirect, browser history, proxy, or log, the attacker still lacks the verifier needed at the token endpoint.

children.label: Verifier → Challenge
children.notes: Generate a fresh high-entropy code_verifier for each authorization request. Send BASE64URL(SHA-256(verifier)) as code_challenge, then send the verifier only during code redemption.

children.label: S256 Only
children.notes: Use code_challenge_method=S256. Do not downgrade to plain when S256 is supported; authorization servers should enforce the original challenge method.

children.label: Use Beyond Public Clients
children.notes: Modern guidance applies PKCE to authorization-code clients generally, including confidential clients. A client secret authenticates the client; PKCE binds the individual authorization transaction.

children.label: Common Mistakes
children.notes: Reusing or logging verifiers, losing the verifier across redirects, accepting a token request without the original challenge, low entropy, or assuming PKCE prevents login CSRF.

children.label: STS & Token Exchange
children.notes: A Security Token Service validates one security context and issues a new, purpose-bound token. OAuth Token Exchange (RFC 8693) standardizes an HTTP/JSON STS for impersonation and delegation across services or trust domains.

children.label: Exchange Request
children.notes: Use grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange with subject_token and its type. Optional actor_token, resource/audience, scope, and requested_token_type express the desired context.

children.label: Subject Token
children.notes: Represents the party on whose behalf the request is made. Validate its token type, issuer, audience, time, signature or introspection result, and whether policy permits exchange.

children.label: Actor Token
children.notes: Optionally represents the acting party receiving delegated rights. The issued token can carry an act claim, including a nested delegation chain.

children.label: Issued Token
children.notes: The response identifies issued_token_type and token_type. The new token has its own lifetime, audience, scope, and revocation behavior; exchange does not automatically invalidate or tightly link the input token.

children.label: Delegation vs Impersonation
children.notes: Impersonation makes the issued credential represent the subject in a limited context. Delegation preserves both subject and actor so the receiver knows who is acting for whom.

children.label: Impersonation
children.notes: The actor operates as the subject within the issued token's rights. Use only when the downstream service does not need actor identity and policy explicitly permits it.

children.label: Delegation
children.notes: The actor remains identifiable while exercising rights delegated by the subject. Preserve and audit both identities; bound delegation chains and prevent confused-deputy behavior.

children.label: Downscoping
children.notes: Every hop should narrow audience, scope, lifetime, and authorization context. Never forward a broad front-end token to multiple services or let exchange amplify privileges.

children.label: Cross-Domain Exchange
children.notes: An STS can bridge token formats, issuers, clouds, or legacy protocols only through explicit trust policy. Translation is not trust: validate the source and issue a new local credential for a precise target.

children.label: Exchange Policy
children.notes: Authorize which clients may exchange which subject/actor tokens for which resources and scopes. Enforce maximum chain depth, no privilege amplification, replay defense, and full subject/actor audit trails.

children.label: On-Behalf-Of (OBO)
children.notes: OBO is an architecture pattern in which API A uses a user's delegated context to obtain a new token for API B. Microsoft names a concrete on_behalf_of grant; standards-oriented platforms commonly model the pattern with RFC 8693 token exchange.

children.label: A → API A → STS → API B
children.notes: The client calls API A with a token whose audience is API A. API A authenticates itself to the STS and presents the user token; the STS issues a new token whose audience is API B.

children.label: Validate Inbound Token
children.notes: API A must validate issuer, API-A audience, time, signature or introspection, sender constraint if present, scopes, tenant, and authorization before requesting another token.

children.label: Authenticate API A
children.notes: API A is a confidential client. Prefer private_key_jwt, mTLS, or managed workload identity over shared secrets; do not confuse API A's identity with the user's identity.

children.label: Issue for API B
children.notes: The downstream access token must target API B, carry only allowed delegated permissions, and preserve user plus actor context when downstream policy or auditing needs both.

children.label: OBO vs App-only
children.notes: Use OBO when downstream authorization depends on the user. Use client credentials when the service acts under its own application permissions. Never invent a user context for a background workload.

children.label: Hop-by-Hop Tokens
children.notes: Each API validates a token intended for itself and exchanges for the next API. Do not relay the original bearer token through the chain; audience restriction limits blast radius.

children.label: Effective Permissions
children.notes: The result should be no broader than the intersection of user delegation, API A's permitted downstream access, tenant policy, consent, and API B's authorization rules.

children.label: OBO Failure Modes
children.notes: Wrong inbound audience, forwarding ID tokens, accepting app-only tokens as users, over-broad downstream scopes, unbounded delegation, missing actor audit, and assuming upstream consent automatically authorizes every downstream API.

children.label: Client & Workload Patterns
children.notes: Client architecture determines where credentials and tokens can safely live. Prefer patterns that keep bearer credentials out of hostile or highly exposed execution contexts.

children.label: Browser + BFF
children.notes: A Backend for Frontend performs code + PKCE as a confidential client, keeps tokens server-side, and gives the browser a hardened session cookie. Protect cookie-authenticated endpoints against CSRF and session fixation.

children.label: Pure SPA
children.notes: A SPA is a public client: use code + PKCE, no embedded secret, short token lifetimes, strict CSP, and avoid persistent browser storage. XSS can still act through the client even when tokens are sender-constrained.

children.label: Native & Desktop
children.notes: Follow RFC 8252: launch the external user-agent, use code + PKCE, prefer claimed HTTPS or loopback redirects where appropriate, and store refresh tokens or keys in platform secure storage.

children.label: Services & Jobs
children.notes: Use client credentials for app-only access or token exchange for delegated access. Prefer short-lived, automatically rotated workload credentials over static secrets.

children.label: Workload Identity Federation
children.notes: Exchange a platform-attested workload credential—such as Kubernetes, cloud, or CI identity—for a short-lived target credential. Bind issuer, subject, audience, repository/environment, and deployment policy tightly.

children.label: Tokens & Validation
children.notes: Tokens are typed, audience-bound protocol artifacts. A JWT is only a serialization format; its validity depends on the issuer, profile, key, claims, intended recipient, and authorization policy.

children.label: Token Types
children.notes: Access tokens authorize APIs; ID tokens inform clients about authentication; refresh tokens obtain new access; authorization codes are one-time exchange artifacts. Do not substitute one for another.

children.label: Access Token
children.notes: May be opaque or structured. The client should treat it as opaque; only the intended API or its validation tier interprets it.

children.label: Refresh Token
children.notes: A high-value credential for the AS token endpoint. Rotate or sender-constrain public-client refresh tokens, detect reuse, and revoke the token family after compromise.

children.label: Opaque vs JWT
children.notes: Opaque tokens centralize validation through introspection and hide claims. JWTs allow local validation but complicate revocation, key rotation, claim freshness, and privacy. Choose from system needs, not convenience.

children.label: JWT Validation Pipeline
children.notes: Select the expected token profile first; pin allowed algorithms; resolve trusted keys; verify signature; validate exact iss, aud, exp, nbf and profile-specific claims; then apply authorization. Reject ambiguous or duplicate semantics.

children.label: Audience, Scope & Subject
children.notes: aud identifies the intended recipient; scope describes delegated capability; sub identifies the represented principal in the issuer's namespace. All three may be necessary but are not sufficient for resource authorization.

children.label: Token Introspection
children.notes: RFC 7662 lets an authorized resource server ask whether a token is active and obtain metadata. Authenticate the caller, restrict disclosures, cache only within risk tolerance, and still enforce audience and authorization.

children.label: Storage & Leakage
children.notes: Never place tokens in URLs or logs. Keep browser tokens in memory or behind a BFF; use OS-protected storage for native apps; encrypt server caches; minimize token lifetime, claims, and propagation.

children.label: Expiry, Revocation & Logout
children.notes: Short-lived access tokens limit replay; RFC 7009 revokes grants or refresh credentials; introspection can provide near-real-time status. Session logout and token revocation are related but not equivalent.

children.label: Hardened OAuth Profiles
children.notes: PKCE protects authorization codes, but high-value ecosystems also protect authorization messages, authenticate clients strongly, and bind tokens to their presenters.

children.label: Client Authentication
children.notes: Confidential clients authenticate at the token endpoint. Prefer asymmetric private_key_jwt or mTLS where practical; rotate keys, validate assertion audience and jti, and avoid long-lived shared secrets.

children.label: private_key_jwt
children.notes: The client signs a short-lived assertion with a registered private key. Validate iss/sub as client_id, token-endpoint audience, time, signature, and replay-resistant jti.

children.label: mTLS Client Auth
children.notes: RFC 8705 uses client certificates for token-endpoint authentication and can certificate-bind access tokens. Plan certificate issuance, rotation, proxy termination, and trust anchors carefully.

children.label: Sender-Constrained Tokens
children.notes: A stolen bearer token can be replayed by whoever possesses it. DPoP or mTLS binds a token to key possession so theft of the token alone is insufficient.

children.label: DPoP
children.notes: RFC 9449 uses a per-request signed proof with htm, htu, iat, jti and, for resource calls, ath. Verify key binding, method/URI, access-token hash, time window, and replay; DPoP is not client authentication.

children.label: mTLS-bound Token
children.notes: The AS binds the token to a certificate thumbprint and the RS verifies the same client certificate. Strong for controlled server environments; operationally harder through gateways and service meshes.

children.label: PAR, JAR & JARM
children.notes: PAR (RFC 9126) pushes the request directly to the AS; JAR (RFC 9101) signs/encrypts request parameters; JARM signs/encrypts authorization responses. Together they reduce front-channel tampering and ambiguity.

children.label: Rich Authorization Requests
children.notes: RAR (RFC 9396) expresses structured authorization_details such as payment amount, account, action, or location. It complements scopes and enables explicit fine-grained consent and policy.

children.label: FAPI 2.0
children.notes: The final OpenID FAPI 2.0 Security Profile combines OAuth Security BCP, PAR, PKCE, strong client authentication, and sender-constrained tokens for high-value APIs. Use the conformance suite rather than assembling an ad hoc subset.

children.label: CIBA
children.notes: Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication decouples the consumption device from user authentication. It suits call-center, decoupled, and headless scenarios; authenticate the client and protect binding/user codes from social engineering.

children.label: Threats & Defenses
children.notes: Use RFC 9700 OAuth Security BCP as the baseline threat model. Most failures are trust-boundary, redirect, replay, validation, or authorization mistakes rather than broken cryptography.

children.label: Login CSRF & State Injection
children.notes: Bind the authorization response to the initiating browser transaction using state or an equivalent framework mechanism, single-use server state, PKCE, and OIDC nonce. Do not accept unsolicited callbacks.

children.label: Authorization Server Mix-up
children.notes: A client talking to multiple issuers can send a code to the wrong token endpoint. Bind the transaction to the expected issuer and validate the issuer identifier in the authorization response and tokens.

children.label: Code Injection & Replay
children.notes: Use PKCE, exact redirects, one-time short-lived codes, transaction binding, and secure callback handling. A code should be redeemable only by the intended client and redirect context.

children.label: Token Theft & Replay
children.notes: Use TLS, prevent logging/leakage, short lifetimes, audience restriction, rotation, and sender-constrained tokens where risk warrants. DPoP/mTLS reduce off-device replay but do not cure XSS or compromised clients.

children.label: Confused Deputy
children.notes: A service must not use its authority for an untrusted caller without validating purpose, subject, audience, and delegated scope. This is central to STS and OBO policy.

children.label: Cross-JWT Confusion
children.notes: Separate validation rules for ID tokens, access tokens, client assertions, logout tokens, DPoP proofs, and authorization responses. Pin typ/profile, issuer, audience, keys, and algorithms; never use one JWT kind where another is expected.

children.label: XSS, CSRF & Cookies
children.notes: CSP, output encoding, dependency hygiene, HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens or origin checks, and session rotation work together. OAuth protocol controls cannot compensate for arbitrary script execution.

children.label: Secret & Key Hygiene
children.notes: Keep secrets out of source, images, URLs, logs, and public clients. Use managed key stores, least-privilege access, automated rotation, overlap for verification keys, and incident-ready revocation.

children.label: Policy & Operations
children.notes: A secure protocol deployment requires lifecycle controls, explicit policy, observability, resilience, privacy, and conformance testing—not only correct happy-path token issuance.

children.label: Authorization Model
children.notes: Combine coarse token capabilities with API-side RBAC, ABAC, ReBAC, or policy-as-code. Centralize policy where consistency matters, but keep enforcement at each resource boundary.

children.label: Audit & Correlation
children.notes: Record issuer, client, subject, actor, tenant, audience, scopes, grant/exchange type, policy decision, token identifier hash, and correlation ID without logging raw tokens. Preserve OBO actor chains for investigation.

children.label: Key & Credential Rotation
children.notes: Automate signing-key publication and overlap, client-key/certificate rollover, secret expiry, emergency revocation, and cache refresh. Test rotation before incidents make it urgent.

children.label: Resilience & Caching
children.notes: Define behavior for AS, JWKS, introspection, policy, and STS outages. Bound caches by credential lifetime and revocation risk; fail closed for authorization without turning transient key rotation into a global outage.

children.label: Privacy & Data Minimization
children.notes: Minimize scopes and claims, use pairwise subjects where appropriate, avoid identity data in URLs/logs, restrict introspection, define retention, and consider correlation created by shared identifiers.

children.label: Conformance & Negative Tests
children.notes: Use certified implementations and OpenID conformance tests where applicable. Test wrong issuer/audience, expired and future tokens, alg/key confusion, replay, redirect variants, scope escalation, token substitution, and delegation-chain abuse.

children.label: Incident Response
children.notes: Prepare to revoke grants and credentials, rotate keys, invalidate sessions, reduce lifetimes, block clients or issuers, trace subject/actor chains, notify relying parties, and recover without reintroducing compromised trust.
